newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan's main Islamist party to boycott poll.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan's main Islamist party to boycott poll.

text.p: Pakistan's main fundamentalist Islamist party, the Jamaat-i-Islami, announced on Sunday that it would boycott a general election set for February 3, accusing the present caretaker government of failing to stem corruption.
Jamaat leader Qazi Hussain Ahmad, speaking to reporters in the Punjab provincial capital of Lahore, said the decision was made by his party's central shura, or council.
At the same time, former prime minister Benazir Bhutto pledged to consider an early general election if the Supreme Court accepted her petition to restore her sacked government.
The Jamaat has been in the forefront of a campaign against Bhutto but has not not done well in past general elections.

Prime Minister Meraj Khalid's 55-day-old caretaker government has come under increasing criticism for apparently failing to produce any concrete evidence of the corruption which President Farooq Leghari had cited in dismissing Bhutto's government on November 5.
Khalid blamed the delay on difficulties in collecting the evidence.
Ahmad said the Jamaat would hold protests across the country but would not resist the planned February poll, for which its nominees had already filed their candidacies.
"The decision not to participate in the election will help promote democratic values," he said. "It will also be helpful in bringing competent and God-fearing leadership to the forefront."
Ahmad also quoted from a Jamaat Shura resolution calling upon citizens to stay away from the polling stations.

His party, which has carried on a bitter rivalry with Bhutto's Pakistan People's Party, won just three seats in the dissolved 217-seat National Assembly at the last general election in October, 1993, when Bhutto came to power.

But, with strong base in student politics, it has shown more skill at mobilising its youthful adherents for confrontations with police and its political opponents. It had earlier enjoyed close ties with the military under late military ruler General Mohammad Zia-ul-Haq.
Since Leghari dismissed the Bhutto government last month on the disputed allegations of corruption and misrule, no charges have been brought against any politician yet.
Bhutto, who denies any wrongdoing, has gone to the Supreme Court with a petition seeking her restoration as prime minister.

She told reporters in Islamabad on Sunday that, if her government were restored, she would consult her main rival and former prime minister Nawaz Sharif to decide whether to hold fresh elections before completing her five-year term in 1997.
Jamaat's boycott decision came a day after Khalid ruled out the possibility of imposing martial law and said his administration would keep to the February 3 voting date.
